title: Seville Orange Marmalade
subtitle: Classic Dundee-cut bitter marmalade, the proper January preserve
excerpt: Seville oranges appear for about six weeks in January and February. Bitter, high in pectin, and the only citrus that gives proper marmalade its characteristic bite. Makes about six 450 g jars from 1 kg of fruit.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton (PG #10136); Pam Corbin, Preserves. Seville orange marmalade is the canonical British marmalade; Dundee-cut refers to medium-thick shreds of peel.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The peel and juice can be prepared the day before and refrigerated in the cooking water overnight — this softens the peel further and means the final cook takes less time.

glossaryTerms.definition: The white spongy layer between the orange skin and the flesh. In marmalade it is packed with pectin and contributes to the set; it is cooked with the pips in muslin.
105 °C for marmalade; higher than jam. Confirmed by the wrinkle test on a chilled plate or a sugar thermometer.

projectSchedule.title: Prepare the peel and pips
projectSchedule.body: Halve the oranges, juice them, and pare the peel from the pith. Shred the peel, tie the pith and pips in muslin, and cover everything with water. Leave overnight.

projectSchedule.title: Cook to setting point and jar
projectSchedule.body: Simmer the peel in the soaking water until completely tender. Add sugar, boil hard to 105 °C, then jar while hot.

content.text: Seville orange marmalade is a two-day project. The peel needs a long, gentle simmer to soften before the sugar goes in. Starting the evening before makes the final cook much shorter. Seville oranges appear for about six weeks in January and February. Their high pectin and bitterness make them the only citrus that gives marmalade its proper bite. Makes about six 450 g jars.

go into muslin and cook with the peel,  they are the primary source of pectin in marmalade. The shredded peel itself adds texture and flavour; the thickness of the shreds is a personal call, but medium-cut (Dundee-style) is the most versatile.
You also need a square of muslin large enough to hold all the pips and pith with room to spare.

Scrub the oranges. Halve and juice them into a bowl,  reserve the juice. Scrape the pith and pips from the orange halves onto the muslin square. Tie into a bundle with string. Cut the peel into shreds to your preferred thickness. Put the shredded peel, the muslin bundle, the juice, and the water into the jam pan. Bring to a simmer, cover, and simmer gently for 1½ hours until the peel is completely soft,  it should collapse when pressed between your fingers. Or, simmer for 1 hour, then leave overnight and continue the next day.
Day two,  add sugar and boil

Lift out the muslin bundle and squeeze it against the side of the pan to extract every drop of pectin-rich liquid. Add the sugar and stir over low heat until completely dissolved. Bring to a full, rapid boil. Cook at a hard boil until the thermometer reads 105 (the
) °C, usually 10 to 20 minutes. Test on a cold plate: push the surface with a fingertip,  it should wrinkle rather than run. If it runs, boil for 3 more minutes and test again.

Take the pan off the heat and skim the foam. Rest for 10 minutes,  this prevents the peel floating to the top of the jars. Stir gently to distribute the peel evenly, then ladle into hot sterilised jars and seal immediately.

items.symptom: Peel is tough and chewy in the finished jar
items.cause: The peel was not softened long enough before the sugar went in. Sugar hardens peel, once in, no further softening occurs.
items.fix: The rule is non-negotiable: peel must be completely soft before sugar is added. Next time simmer for longer at the first stage.

items.cause: Insufficient pectin extraction, or the boil wasn't hot enough.
items.fix: Return to the pan, squeeze the muslin bundle hard to extract more pectin, boil again and use a thermometer, reach 105 °C.

items.symptom: Peel floats to the top of the jar
items.cause: Jarred too soon after reaching setting point.
items.fix: Rest the pan off the heat for 10 minutes and stir before ladling. This distributes the peel evenly as the marmalade begins to cool and thicken.

items.symptom: Marmalade is bitter rather than pleasantly sharp
items.cause: Pith from the peel entered the shreds during cutting.
items.fix: When shredding the peel, score and remove any thick white pith from the inner side. A thin skin of pith attached is fine; thick clumps cause bitterness.

content.text: 12 months sealed in a cool, dark place. Refrigerate once opened.
